title: Understanding Direct Indexing & Thematic Stock Baskets
description: Pros, cons, and use cases for 'Custom Indexing' (like Smallcase/M1 Finance).
content:
For decades, investors had two choices: buy a pre-made ETF (like VTI) or pick individual stocks. Now, technology offers a third way: **Direct Indexing** (often called 'Baskets' or 'Pies'). Platforms like M1 Finance, Fidelity Solo FidFolios, and Wealthfront allow you to buy a basket of 50 stocks with one click. This allows for 'Thematic Investing' (e.g., buying a 'Green Energy' basket) or tax optimization without the fees of an active fund. This guide explores whether you should build your own index or stick to ETFs.

Key Takeaways

  • Customization: Don't like that the S&P 500 holds tobacco companies? With Direct Indexing, you can buy the S&P 500 minus the tobacco stocks. You control the holdings.
  • Tax Loss Harvesting: This is the killer feature. In an ETF, you can't sell the losers inside the fund. In a Direct Index, you own the individual stocks. You can sell just the losers (e.g., Ford) to harvest tax losses while keeping the winners (e.g., Tesla).
  • Complexity Cost: Owning 50 stocks means getting a tax document with 50 dividend payments. It adds administrative weight to your life.
  • Thematic Risks: Buying a 'Electric Vehicle' basket is still a sector bet. If the sector crashes, you crash. It is riskier than a broad market ETF.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Direct Indexing used to require $500,000 minimums. Technology has lowered this to $5,000 (Wealthfront) or even $100 (M1 Finance). It is the fastest-growing segment of retail wealth management.

ETF vs. Direct Indexing

Should you unbundle the ETF?

The ETF Structure (VTI)

Pros: Simple. One ticker. One tax line item. Low fee (0.03%).
Cons: You can't control what's inside. You can't harvest losses on individual stocks inside the fund.

The Direct Index Structure (The Basket)

Pros: You own the actual shares of Apple, Microsoft, etc.
Tax Alpha: If the market is flat but Apple is up and Microsoft is down, you can sell Microsoft to bank a tax loss. In an ETF, you couldn't do this.
Cons: Fees. Some platforms charge monthly fees ($3-$5) or AUM fees (0.25%) for this service. This can outweigh the tax benefit for small accounts.

Best Use Cases

  1. The 'ESG' Investor: If you hate oil companies but want S&P 500 returns, Direct Indexing allows you to build 'S&P 500 ex-Oil'.
  2. The High Earner: If you have a large taxable account ($100k+), the tax-loss harvesting benefits of Direct Indexing can save you thousands in taxes, justifying the complexity.
  3. The Concentrated Employee: If you work at Google and have tons of Google stock, you don't want to buy an S&P 500 fund (which is heavy on Google). Direct Indexing lets you buy 'S&P 500 ex-Google' to diversify.
  4. The Beginner Warning: If you have <$50k, stick to ETFs. The tax benefits of Direct Indexing aren't powerful enough to justify the hassle/fees on small balances.

Frequently Asked Questions

What platforms do this?

M1 Finance: Uses 'Pies'. Free. Great for DIY.
Fidelity Solo FidFolios: $5/month.
Wealthfront: 0.25% fee. Fully automated tax harvesting.

Is it harder to file taxes?

Yes. Your 1099-B will be hundreds of pages long because you sold individual stocks. TurboTax handles it, but it's intimidating.

Can I beat the market this way?

Unlikely. Direct Indexing is usually about matching the market while saving on taxes, not picking winners. It is a tax play, not an alpha play.
